title: Caching with Redis
summary: A cache-aside setup: the app asks Redis first and falls back to Postgres. Play the flows to see a hit, a miss, a write, a stampede, a stale read, a Redis outage and an eviction. Latencies are in-datacenter figures; the client hop is counted as in-DC too, to keep totals comparable.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.what: Sends HTTP requests such as GET /users/42 and PUT /users/42.
nodes.why: The thing the whole system is tuned for: users feel the latency of every request.
nodes.gotcha: Clients also cache (browser cache, HTTP Cache-Control). That is a separate layer with its own staleness.

nodes.label: App server
nodes.what: Runs the cache-aside logic: check Redis, on a miss read Postgres and fill Redis, on a write update Postgres and delete the key.
nodes.why: The app owns the caching policy because it knows how to build, serialize and key the data. Redis only stores what it is handed.
nodes.gotcha: Every caller must follow the same pattern and the same key names. One code path that writes to the DB without deleting the key leaves stale data.
pros: Cache failure degrades instead of breaking reads
cons: Caching logic lives in application code
A miss costs three round trips (GET, SELECT, SET)

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.what: An in-memory key-value store. Reads cost about 0.2 to 0.5 ms round trip in the same datacenter, with the lookup itself well under a millisecond.
nodes.why: Memory is roughly 100x to 1000x faster than a database query and takes read load off Postgres.
nodes.gotcha: It is a copy, not the truth. Memory is finite (maxmemory), so keys are evicted, and keys expire (TTL), so a missing key never means the data does not exist.
cons: Extra system to run and monitor
nodes.body: Click the box to read how maxmemory-policy and TTL expiry decide what stays.

nodes.label: Postgres
nodes.what: Holds the durable data. A primary-key lookup with a warm buffer pool takes about 1 to 5 ms; a cold or contended query takes 10 ms or more.
nodes.why: The only place a write is truly safe. Everything else can be rebuilt from here.
nodes.gotcha: It has a connection and CPU ceiling. A cache outage or stampede shifts the full read load here and can take it down.
pros: Transactions and a single version of the truth
cons: Hard to scale reads without replicas

nodes.label: Change stream
nodes.what: Carries a message for every committed row change (change data capture from the write-ahead log, or an outbox table).
nodes.why: Lets invalidation happen after commit and be retried, instead of depending on the app's one DEL.
nodes.gotcha: Delivery is at-least-once and slightly delayed (tens to hundreds of ms). Deleting a key twice is harmless; that is why DEL suits it.
cons: A short window of staleness remains

nodes.label: Invalidator
nodes.what: Reads change messages and deletes the matching cache keys.
nodes.why: Moves cache invalidation out of the request path, so a slow or failed Redis does not fail a write.
nodes.gotcha: Messages for the same row must be handled in order, or a late DEL can race a refill the same way a reader can.

edges.label: GET /users/42
edges.what: The user request and its response.

edges.label: GET / SET / DEL
edges.what: Cache commands. RESP is the Redis wire protocol; each command is one round trip, about 0.2 to 0.5 ms in the same datacenter.

edges.label: SELECT / UPDATE
edges.what: Reads on a miss, and every write.

edges.label: row change event
edges.what: Committed changes published asynchronously; nobody waits for them.

edges.label: consume
edges.what: The invalidator pulls events from the stream.

edges.label: DEL user:42
edges.what: Invalidation driven by the database's own change log.

flows.title: Read · cache hit
flows.summary: The key is in Redis. The app never touches Postgres: about 1 ms end to end.

steps.title: Request arrives
steps.does: The client asks for user 42. The app derives the cache key user:42 from the URL.

steps.title: App asks Redis first
steps.does: One command on a pooled connection. No SQL, no disk.

steps.title: Redis looks the key up
steps.does: A hash table lookup in memory, plus a TTL check. The key exists and has not expired.
steps.note: The lookup is microseconds. The cost you pay is the network round trip, not the memory access.

steps.title: Value returns
steps.does: Redis sends the serialized value back.

steps.title: App builds the response
steps.does: Deserialize the JSON and write the HTTP response. Postgres was never involved.

steps.title: Response to the client
steps.does: 200 OK with the user.
steps.note: Total about 0.95 ms, versus about 14 ms for the miss path. At a 95% hit ratio the database sees only 1 request in 20.

flows.title: Read · cache miss
flows.summary: The key is absent. The app reads Postgres, fills Redis with a TTL, and replies. About 14 ms, roughly 15x slower than a hit.

steps.title: Request arrives
steps.does: Same request as before, but nobody has read user 42 for a while.

steps.title: App asks Redis first
steps.does: Always the same first move, hit or miss.

steps.title: Redis has nothing
steps.does: The key does not exist. Redis answers with a nil reply.
steps.note: A miss is not an error. Redis cannot tell whether the key expired, was evicted or never existed.

steps.title: Fall back to Postgres
steps.does: The app runs the real query on the source of truth.

steps.title: Postgres executes the query
steps.does: Primary-key index lookup, heap fetch, possibly a buffer pool miss that goes to SSD. Plan, parse and commit overheads add up.
steps.note: This is the work the cache exists to avoid. 12 ms here is a busy but healthy database.

steps.title: Row comes back
steps.does: One row, version 7.

steps.title: Fill the cache with a TTL
steps.does: SET with EX makes the write and the expiry one atomic command. Without a TTL the key could live forever and go stale forever.

steps.title: Redis confirms
steps.does: OK. The app does not need to wait for this to answer the user, but most clients do.

steps.title: App builds the response
steps.does: Serialize and write the HTTP response.

steps.title: Response to the client
steps.does: 200 OK with the user.
steps.note: Total about 14.25 ms. The next reader of user:42 pays only about 1 ms.

whatifs.title: a hot key expires under load (stampede)
whatifs.summary: Many requests miss at the same instant and all go to Postgres.

steps.title: A hot key expires
steps.does: user:42 serves 2,000 reads per second. Its TTL runs out. For the next 12 ms, the time one query takes to refill it, every request misses.

steps.title: Everyone misses
steps.does: In the next 12 ms about 24 requests arrive, on many app servers. Each runs GET, gets nil, and decides to refill the cache.

steps.title: All of them query Postgres
steps.does: Identical SELECTs, 24 at once. Each one is wasted work, because only one result is needed.

steps.title: Database queues up
steps.does: A burst of identical queries competes for CPU and connections. Latency climbs, and slow queries make more requests miss while waiting.
steps.note: One hot key becomes a database outage. This is a cache stampede or thundering herd. It gets worse with more traffic and slower queries.

steps.title: Everyone writes the same value
steps.does: Each request finishes and issues the same SET. 24 redundant writes, all with the same TTL, so they expire together again.

state.name: user:42
state.note: TTL 300 s, will expire in sync again

whatifs.title: the fix: one request refills, the rest wait
whatifs.summary: A short lock lets only one request hit Postgres.

steps.title: Everyone misses, as before
steps.does: The key expired and 24 requests arrive. This time each one tries to take a lock before touching the database.

steps.title: Try to take the lock
steps.does: SET with NX only succeeds if the key does not exist, and PX gives it a timeout so a crashed holder cannot block forever. The value is a random token that identifies the owner.

state.name: lock:user:42
state.note: TTL 5000 ms, held by one request

steps.title: One wins, 23 lose
steps.does: The winner gets OK. The other 23 get nil from SET NX. They do not query the database; they wait about 50 ms and read the cache again, or serve a stale copy if you keep one.

steps.title: Only the winner queries Postgres
steps.does: One SELECT instead of 24.

steps.title: Database stays calm
steps.does: A single normal-cost query.

steps.title: Winner fills the cache and releases the lock
steps.does: SET the value with TTL 300 plus a few seconds of random jitter, then delete the lock only if the token still matches (a small Lua script), so a slow holder never deletes someone else's lock.

steps.title: Waiters retry and hit
steps.does: The 23 waiting requests read the cache again and find the value.
steps.note: Other defenses: request coalescing inside one app process (single-flight per key), jitter on TTLs so keys do not expire together, and early probabilistic refresh, where a reader refreshes a key slightly before its TTL ends with rising probability.

flows.title: Write · update DB, delete key
flows.summary: Write to Postgres first, then DELETE the cache key. The next read refills it. Delete, not update, because a delete can never leave a wrong value behind.

steps.title: Write arrives
steps.does: The client changes the user's plan from pro to team.

steps.title: Update the source of truth first
steps.does: The write goes to Postgres inside a transaction. Until it commits, no one else can see it.
steps.carries: UPDATE users SET plan='team', version=8 WHERE id=42

values.name: sql
values.value: UPDATE users SET plan = 'team', version = 8 WHERE id = 42

steps.title: Commit
steps.does: The row is written and flushed to the write-ahead log. After this the change is durable.
steps.note: Cache and DB now disagree: Redis still says pro. This is the stale window, and it lasts until the next step.

steps.title: Postgres confirms
steps.does: 1 row updated.

steps.title: Delete the cache key
steps.does: DEL removes the stale copy. The app does not write the new value here; the next reader will load it from the database.
steps.note: Deleting is idempotent and safe to repeat. Setting the new value instead risks overwriting a newer one if two writers interleave; a delete just forces a fresh read.

steps.title: Key removed
steps.does: Redis frees the entry.

steps.title: Redis confirms
steps.does: The reply is the number of keys deleted.

steps.title: Write succeeds
steps.does: 200 OK. The write path costs one DB write plus one DEL.

steps.title: Next read repopulates
steps.does: The next GET /users/42 misses, reads version 8 from Postgres and runs SET EX 300, exactly like the read-miss flow.
steps.note: The first reader after a write pays the miss. Hot keys that are written often have poor hit ratios; consider not caching them.

whatifs.title: a slow reader refills with an old value
whatifs.summary: A read and a write interleave so the cache ends up holding version 7 after the delete.

steps.title: Key is absent
steps.does: user:42 just expired. A reader and a writer arrive at nearly the same time.

steps.title: Reader A misses
steps.does: Reader A runs GET and gets nil.

steps.title: Reader A reads the old row
steps.does: A's SELECT runs just before the writer commits, so it sees version 7. Then A stalls briefly, for example on a GC pause or a slow network hop.

steps.title: Writer B commits version 8
steps.does: Writer B updates and commits while A is stalled.

steps.title: B deletes the key, finds nothing
steps.does: B's DEL runs before A has written anything, so there is nothing to delete.
steps.note: The invalidation already happened. It cannot clean up what A is about to write.

steps.title: A fills the cache with version 7
steps.does: A finally runs its SET with the value it read earlier.

state.name: user:42
state.note: STALE. DB has v8. Lives until TTL, 300 s

steps.title: Everyone now reads stale data
steps.does: Every reader hits the cache and gets plan pro. The hit ratio looks perfect while the data is wrong.
steps.note: The TTL is the safety net: it bounds the wrongness to 300 s. This race is rare, because it needs a reader slower than a write, but at scale it will happen.

steps.title: Fix 1: delayed double delete
steps.does: After the write, the writer deletes the key again after a short delay (for example 500 ms, longer than a slow read). That second DEL removes a stale refill.

state.name: user:42
state.note: second delete cleared the stale v7

steps.title: Fix 2: versioned values
steps.does: Store the row version in the value and refill with a compare-and-set (a Lua script or WATCH/MULTI): only write if the new version is higher than the cached one. A stale v7 can never overwrite v8. Fix 3, driven by CDC, is in the next what-if.

whatifs.title: the DEL fails
whatifs.summary: Postgres committed, but the app could not delete the key.

steps.title: DEL times out
steps.does: Redis is slow or a network blip drops the command. The app has already committed to Postgres.

state.name: user:42
state.note: STALE. DB has v8. TTL 180 s left

steps.title: The write still succeeds
steps.does: The DB is the truth and it is updated, so the app returns 200. Failing the write would only add inconsistency.

steps.title: Readers see old data
steps.does: Every read hits version 7 until the TTL expires. Nothing else repairs it.
steps.note: This is why every key needs a TTL. A key without one stays wrong until someone notices.

steps.title: Retry the invalidation
steps.does: Retry the DEL with backoff, or write an outbox row in the same DB transaction so a worker retries until it succeeds. CDC (next what-if) does this for you.

whatifs.title: delete first, then update (wrong order)
whatifs.summary: Deleting before the DB write lets a concurrent reader refill the old value.

steps.title: Writer deletes the key first
steps.does: The writer removes the key before touching Postgres, thinking it is cleaning up in advance.

steps.title: A reader misses
steps.does: A concurrent reader finds the key gone.

steps.title: The reader reads the old row
steps.does: The writer has not committed yet, so the reader gets version 7.

steps.title: The reader refills the cache with v7
steps.does: SET user:42 with the old value and a fresh TTL.

steps.title: The writer commits version 8
steps.does: Now the DB has v8 and the cache has v7, with nothing left to delete the key.
steps.note: The order is DB first, then delete. With the correct order, the reader's window is far smaller and the TTL covers the rest.

whatifs.title: invalidate from the change log (CDC)
whatifs.summary: The app only writes to Postgres. A worker deletes the key from the database's own change stream.

steps.title: App answers right away
steps.does: The app does not touch Redis on the write path. It returns once Postgres has committed.

steps.title: Postgres emits a change event
steps.does: The write-ahead log is read by a CDC connector (for example Debezium), or an outbox row is published. The event says table users, id 42, version 8.

steps.title: Invalidator consumes it
steps.does: At-least-once delivery. If the worker crashes before acking, the message is delivered again.

steps.title: Worker deletes the key
steps.does: DEL is idempotent, so redelivery is harmless. If Redis is down, the worker retries until it is back.
steps.note: Invalidation is driven by committed data, so no code path can forget it, and it is retried. The cost is a short delay, here about 25 ms, and extra infrastructure. It still needs a TTL as a backstop.

flows.title: Redis is down
flows.summary: The cache node dies. The app must fail fast and fall back to Postgres. Reads keep working, but database load jumps 20x.

steps.title: Normal traffic arrives
steps.does: 10,000 requests per second, 95% served by Redis, so Postgres sees about 500 queries per second.

steps.title: Redis becomes unreachable
steps.does: The node crashes, restarts empty, or the network drops. No replies come back.

state.name: status
state.note: all keys lost if it was a crash without persistence

steps.title: GET times out
steps.does: The app waits for a reply. With a tight timeout (20 to 50 ms) a failing call is cheap. With the default of several seconds, threads pile up and the app falls over too.
steps.note: Set connect and read timeouts explicitly. A hung dependency is worse than a dead one.

steps.title: Circuit breaker opens
steps.does: After several failures in a row the app stops calling Redis for about 10 seconds, then lets a single probe through. Later requests skip the 50 ms wait entirely.

steps.title: Fall back to Postgres
steps.does: Treat the cache error as a miss and read the source of truth. The app stays correct, only slower.

steps.title: Database absorbs everything
steps.does: Every request now runs SQL. Under the higher load queries run slower.
steps.note: The cache was not only an optimization; the database was sized assuming 95% of reads never reach it.

steps.title: Rows come back, slowly
steps.does: Responses still arrive but at several times the normal latency. Slow responses tie up connections, which slows everyone further.

steps.title: Users still get answers
steps.does: Degraded but working.
steps.note: If the DB tips over the whole site goes down, and restarting Redis empty makes it worse. Defenses: load shedding or rate limiting, a small in-process cache of the hottest keys, replicas or Redis Cluster so a node failure loses only a slice of keys, and persistence or a warm standby.

steps.title: Redis returns, cold
steps.does: It is back but empty. The breaker probes, succeeds and closes, and every request now misses and refills, which hammers the DB again for a while.
steps.note: Warm the cache before sending it full traffic: pre-load the hottest keys, ramp traffic gradually, and use the single-flight lock from the stampede fix.

flows.title: Cache full · LRU eviction
flows.summary: Redis hits maxmemory, so a new key forces the least recently used one out. For clarity the cache holds only 3 keys; real instances hold millions.

steps.title: A full cache
steps.does: maxmemory is reached with 3 keys. Config: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru. Notes show how long each key has been idle.

steps.title: A read touches user:2
steps.does: Every access updates the key's last-used clock. user:2 jumps from middle to newest.

steps.title: A new key arrives
steps.does: A miss for user:4 was filled from Postgres. The SET needs memory the cache does not have.

steps.title: Redis evicts the LRU key
steps.does: Before accepting the write Redis frees memory. With allkeys-lru it samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) and removes the one idle longest, here user:1. This is approximate LRU, not an exact list.
steps.note: Eviction frees space by removing keys that may still be valid. TTL expiry removes keys that are due. See the eviction page for the policies.

steps.title: Redis accepts the write
steps.does: OK. With noeviction instead, this SET would have failed with an out-of-memory error.

steps.title: Later, user:1 is requested
steps.does: The key was evicted, not expired. The app cannot tell the difference and sees a plain miss.
steps.note: A rising evicted_keys count together with a falling hit ratio means the cache is too small for the working set.

steps.title: Refilling user:1 evicts the next oldest
steps.does: SET user:1 forces another eviction. The oldest remaining key is user:3.
